sections.h2: What is a good HRV for my age?
sections.body: There is no single good HRV number. The largest published age-by-sex dataset, from about 8 million Fitbit users (Natarajan 2020), shows how RMSSD between 6 and 7 a.m. was spread: the median was {{f20}} ms for women and {{m20}} ms for men at 20–21, {{f40}} and {{m40}} ms at 40–41, and {{f60}} and {{m60}} ms at 60–61. The spread within one age group is wider than the gap between age groups, so a single comparison says little on its own. HRV tends to fall with age; fitness, sleep and regular slow breathing affect where you sit. The more useful question is whether your own HRV holds steady or rises against your baseline. Full guide: [Normal HRV by age](/articles/normal-hrv-by-age).

Apple Watch shows SDNN, not RMSSD, from short readings of about a minute taken several times a day and at night. SDNN and RMSSD are different measures, so the Fitbit table above does not apply to Apple Watch numbers, and this calculator does not compare them. Compare your own 7-day average in the Health app with your earlier weeks instead. If your average drifts well below your usual level for several days, that says more than any one number. More: [Why your HRV differs on every device](/articles/hrv-different-every-device).

A low reading is usually about the last day or two, not your health. The most common causes are alcohol (even one or two drinks lower overnight HRV), short or poor sleep, a late heavy meal, illness coming on, hard training without recovery, dehydration and stress. Your device and genetics also matter: some healthy people simply run lower. Look at the pattern. One low night after a party means little; HRV that stays below your usual range for several days — especially with a higher resting heart rate — suggests your body is under more load than it's handling. Read more: [how much alcohol lowers HRV](/articles/how-much-alcohol-lowers-hrv), [what to do after a low HRV reading](/articles/what-to-do-after-low-hrv-reading) and [overtraining: HRV and resting heart rate](/articles/overtraining-hrv-resting-heart-rate). If a low HRV comes with symptoms such as chest pain, fainting or breathlessness, see a doctor.

HRV rises when your body recovers well, so the levers are about recovery, not hacks. The ones with the most evidence: regular sleep at consistent times, less alcohol (especially in the three hours before bed), aerobic training such as Zone 2 cardio, and managing chronic stress. Slow breathing at about six breaths a minute raises HRV while you practise it, and regular practice over weeks is linked to better resting HRV and baroreflex function. Expect change over weeks, not days, and judge it by your 7-day average. Guides: [how to raise HRV naturally](/articles/how-to-raise-hrv-naturally) and [coherent breathing](/articles/coherent-breathing-guide).

HRV and resting heart rate tell you related but different things. Resting heart rate is how many times your heart beats per minute at rest; HRV is how much the time between beats varies. A higher HRV and a lower resting heart rate usually go together and point to good recovery and fitness. When you're stressed, ill or under-recovered, resting heart rate tends to rise and HRV to fall — often at the same time, which is a stronger signal than either alone. Resting heart rate is simpler, steadier and easier to compare between devices; HRV reacts faster and is more sensitive to sleep, alcohol and stress. Track both against your own baseline. Check yours: [resting heart rate by age](/articles/resting-heart-rate-by-age).

faq.q: What is a good HRV for my age?
faq.a: Among about 8 million Fitbit users, median RMSSD between 6 and 7 a.m. was {{f20}} ms for women and {{m20}} ms for men at 20–21, {{f40}} and {{m40}} ms at 40–41, and {{f60}} and {{m60}} ms at 60–61. That describes the users of one device, not a medical norm. Your own trend matters more than any average.

It takes the published table of morning RMSSD among Fitbit users (Natarajan 2020), picks the age group nearest to your age for your sex, and tells you whether your number is below the middle half, within it, or above it. It does not estimate values between age groups and does not give a percentile.

faq.q: Can I use it with Apple Watch?
faq.a: No. Apple Watch shows SDNN, a different HRV measure from short readings, so it cannot be compared with an RMSSD table. Compare your Apple Watch 7-day average with your own earlier weeks instead.
Usually because of recent alcohol, short or poor sleep, illness, hard training or stress. A single low reading means little; HRV that stays below your usual range for several days is worth attention.

faq.q: How do I raise my HRV?
faq.a: Sleep regularly, cut alcohol (especially near bedtime), do aerobic training such as Zone 2, manage stress and practise slow breathing at about six breaths a minute. Changes show over weeks, not days.

A single low value is not a medical event — it usually reflects sleep, alcohol or training. HRV that stays low against your own baseline can signal accumulated stress or under-recovery. This calculator is educational, not a diagnosis; see a doctor for symptoms.

faq.q: Why does my HRV change so much from day to day?
faq.a: HRV is sensitive to sleep, alcohol, meals, stress, illness and training. Day-to-day swings of 10–20 ms are normal, so compare weekly averages rather than single nights.

faq.q: Where do these numbers come from?
faq.a: From one published study of about 8 million Fitbit users (Natarajan 2020, Lancet Digital Health, Supplementary Table S3): RMSSD measured by the wrist sensor between 6 and 7 a.m. while the wearer was still, by self-reported age and sex. Three of the four authors were Fitbit employees and Fitbit funded the study. It is the distribution among users of one device, not a medical norm.

methodology: Where the numbers come from: one published study, Natarajan et al. 2020 (Lancet Digital Health), Supplementary appendix Table S3 — RMSSD between 6 and 7 a.m. among about 8 million Fitbit users, measured by the wrist optical sensor (PPG) during still periods on one day, with self-reported age and sex. The table gives the median and the 25th–75th percentile for two-year age groups (20–21, 25–26 … 60–61), separately for women and men. Three of the four authors were Fitbit employees and Fitbit funded the study. Fitbit users are not a random sample of the population, other devices and chest-strap ECGs give different numbers, and there are no data under 20 or over 61. How we use it: we pick the age group nearest to your age (ages 18–19 use 20–21, ages over 61 use 60–61) and do not interpolate between groups. Below the 25th percentile we say "lower than most", above the 75th "higher than most", otherwise "within the middle half". This is a comparison with users of one device, not a medical norm or a diagnosis.
